A retained directory capability prevents a replaced parent path or symlink from redirecting publication. It cannot guarantee lexical containment if an external process with filesystem permissions renames the opened directory itself outside the vault while creation is in progress; canonical root resolution and root-handle acquisition also remain separate operations.

A process with write access to the vault can race a staging leaf between identity verification and path-based hard-link or unlink calls. The code verifies the retained file identity and published target immediately before commit, but portable path APIs cannot bind these namespace operations to the retained file handle. A detected staging-name swap can leave an unexpected target or staging entry and require explicit recovery.

Any pre-existing staging entry without a retained identity from the current process is preserved unless recovery proves it is the committed target's hard link. Partial or exact-revision bytes alone do not establish ownership, so ambiguous entries remain for explicit recovery.

same-file identity checks can be ambiguous on some Windows filesystems, including ReFS configurations with non-unique 64-bit file IDs. Publication checks combine identity with revision hashes, but the identity check is not a universal filesystem proof.

Directory-entry durability is best-effort across platforms: Unix syncs the vault parent directory, while the standard Windows API path does not provide a portable directory flush. App-data history writes sync file contents but do not fsync all containing directories. The implementation promises process-interruption recovery, not universal power-loss durability.
